Widows
WID-ohz
noun (bereaved women under God's special care)
From the Old English widewe, akin to Latin vidua; women bereaved of their husbands, set in Scripture under the special protection of God and the duty of His people.

📖 Biblical Definition

Widows are women bereaved of their husbands, whom Scripture places under the special protection of God and the particular care of His people. The LORD names Himself “a father of the fatherless, and a judge of the widows”; He pleads their cause, defends them against oppression, and threatens His wrath upon those who afflict them. Pure religion before God, says James, is to visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction. The early church organized its mercy around this duty: when the widows of the Grecians were neglected in the daily ministration, the apostles appointed the seven, the seed of the diaconate, to serve the tables. Paul gives the church careful rule: honour widows that are widows indeed—the truly destitute and godly, who trust in God and continue in supplications—while charging families first to provide for their own, lest the church be burdened and natural duty neglected. The dictionary marks the care of widows as a non-negotiable mark of true religion and a chief work of the church's mercy, against two errors. The first is the neglect that leaves the bereaved to want while the church spends on itself—a neglect God Himself avenges. The second is the modern outsourcing of all such mercy to the state, as though the family and the church were relieved of a duty Scripture lays squarely upon them. God is the defender of widows; His people are His hands.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Women bereaved of their husbands, under God's special protection (Psalm 68:5) and the church's particular care (James 1:27; 1 Timothy 5:3); their relief a mark of pure religion, neglected at the peril of God's wrath.

expand to see more

WIDOWS, noun. [Old English widewe.] Women bereaved of their husbands.

God is “a father of the fatherless, and a judge of the widows” (Psalm 68:5).

Pure religion visits the fatherless and widows in their affliction (James 1:27).

The church is to honour widows that are widows indeed (1 Timothy 5:3).

The neglect of widows occasioned the appointing of the seven (Acts 6:1).

📖 Key Scripture

Jas 1:27 — "Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world."

1 Ti 5:3 — "Honour widows that are widows indeed."

Ps 68:5 — "A father of the fatherless, and a judge of the widows, is God in his holy habitation."

Ac 6:1 — "And in those days, when the number of the disciples was multiplied, there arose a murmuring of the Grecians against the Hebrews, because their widows were neglected in the daily ministration."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The church errs by neglecting widows while spending on itself; the modern age errs by outsourcing all such mercy to the state, as though family and church were relieved of a duty Scripture lays on them.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the care of widows as a mark of true religion. The first corruption is plain neglect—a church that spends on its own comfort while the bereaved among it want. God names this an offense He avenges, for He is the judge of the widows and hears the cry of the oppressed. The neglect of the Grecian widows nearly fractured the early church and forced the appointing of the seven; the dictionary holds the relief of widows to be a chief and non-negotiable work of the church's mercy.

The second and modern corruption is the outsourcing of all such mercy to the state, as though family and church were relieved of the duty by the welfare office. Scripture orders it otherwise: families are to provide first for their own widows, that the church be not charged; and the church is to honour and relieve those who are widows indeed. The dictionary recovers the layered biblical pattern—family, then church—against both the cold individualism that says “not my concern” and the lazy collectivism that says “let the government do it.” God is the defender of widows, and His people, not the bureaucracy, are appointed His hands.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From the Old English widewe and Latin vidua; the Hebrew 'almanah and Greek chera name the bereaved woman whom God defends and the church relieves.

expand to see more

Widewe, Old English, a widow, akin to Latin vidua (bereft).

'Almanah, Hebrew, a widow, one of the classes of the defenseless God protects.

Chera, Greek, a widow, the object of the church's ordered care (1 Timothy 5).

“Widows indeed” (Greek ontos chera), the truly destitute and godly widow.

The neglect of widows occasioned the diaconate (Acts 6:1-6).

Usage

"The deacons made the relief of widows a first charge, as the early church had done."

"The pastor preached that to neglect the bereaved while spending on comfort is a sin God avenges."

"She honoured the widow indeed, while urging the family to provide first for its own."
